stories.headline: Tesla starts rolling out FSD v15: 25x better on safety-critical cases, plus Tesla Reality View
stories.why_read: Your whole feed last night was v15 clips, and you bookmarked Tesla's release notes plus Sawyer's breakdown: the biggest FSD jump in a long time just hit cars.
body: Tesla says FSD v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. The headline claim is 25x better handling of safety-critical cases. It also adds Tesla Reality View, a live visualization of the drive that lets you see and control what FSD is planning to do, and start-of-trip and end-of-trip navigation that now learns end-to-end from fleet route preferences, with later v15 releases extending that to the whole route.

The smaller items matter for daily driving: better detection of signs, animals, debris, potholes and standing water; more natural speed handling in school zones and bad weather; slowing for speed cameras; and a Bike Rack Mode that lets FSD run with a hitch accessory attached. Sawyer Merritt adds that upcoming turns now show directly in the visualization and turn signals are quieter, fading out after a few clicks.

stories.headline: The Lean and Mathlib communities certify Alpöge's 17-million-line proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.why_read: Yesterday it was a claim. Today the Lean community says it has full confidence the proof is correct, and you retweeted Aaron Levie on why that changes how problems get solved.
body: In a joint statement endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, the Lean and Mathlib communities say Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, released November 20 as a Lean library of 17 million lines, is correct. Dozens of people reproduced the compilation, two independent tools confirmed the proved theorem is exactly Mathlib's statement of RH, and the exported proof passed Lean's kernel plus several independent checkers, two of which come with a formal proof that they cannot accept a false proof. The checks ran on an inert export, out of reach of any malicious code in the sources.

Aaron Levie, in a post you retweeted, quotes the line that captures why this is unsettling: the proof is "something much weirder and more alien" than theory-building, a "wormhole" through 25,000 pages of existing math that no human brain could build alone, and that no current AI could build alone either. The certification settles correctness; the community still has to work out what the new ideas actually are.

stories.headline: Reality View is rendered by the driving model itself, on half of one AI4 accelerator
stories.why_read: You bookmarked both posts: this is the AI story hiding inside the FSD release.
body: Ashok Elluswamy says the same end-to-end driving model that drives the car also renders the realistic view of the world around it. It is not there just to look cool, he writes: it communicates intent, with arrows for the turns FSD plans to take and pins for the spot it intends to park in.

Elon Musk added that this is real-time AI video generation, with no game engine, running on just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Sawyer Merritt notes the view streams from an arbitrary virtual camera above the car, which is why owners are suddenly posting clips that look like a video game.

stories.headline: A pill for advanced pancreatic cancer is hailed as the biggest breakthrough in decades
stories.why_read: Over 1,000 points on Hacker News, and the kind of science-meets-kindness story your pinned post asks for.
body: In a trial of 61 people recently diagnosed with pancreatic cancer that had already spread, the pill daraxonrasib stopped tumors growing in 90% of patients, shrank or eliminated them in just over 60%, and made them undetectable on CT scans in about 8%, The Guardian reports. A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive, against the usual 40-45% on chemotherapy alone.

Doctors stress it is not yet a cure and nobody knows how long it holds the disease off, but Memorial Sloan Kettering's Dr Wungki Park, who presented the results, called it "the closest to cure" and said he had never seen so many tumors disappear in patients whose cancer had spread. Half of people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, so more time is a very big deal.

stories.headline: LookAtMyQuant squeezes Inkling 2 Mini into 5.4 GB for Apple Silicon
stories.why_read: Yesterday's open-weights model is already phone-sized: a quantization compiler worth understanding if you run models locally.
body: LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler: it measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed, then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage. The author has now compressed Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights into six MLX builds for Apple Silicon, from 3.85 GB (aimed at 8 GB iPhones) through 5.38 GB up to 12.76 GB.

The same recipe, per the README, takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB at 2.3 bits per weight for about $34 of GPU time, and Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB while solving as many of its 540 math test problems as the original. Everything is MIT licensed.

stories.headline: Musk warns of an AI cash crunch next year: hundreds of billions just for working capital
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the builder of Colossus saying the hard part is no longer buying GPUs.
body: "Getting this amount of compute turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," Elon Musk wrote. Even a few months of cumulative industry delay between paying for compute and getting it reliable enough to earn revenue, he argues, means hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. "Where will that come from?"

X's news summary puts it in context: AI spending added 1.27 points to US GDP growth over the first three quarters of 2026, about 65% of the total, while Nvidia shares have dropped sharply on funding worries. François Chollet, meanwhile, points to HBM and DRAM sold out through 2029.

stories.headline: NBER study: AI agents drove 240% more commits but only 30% more releases, and users stayed flat
stories.why_read: A sober data point for anyone running developer platforms: output exploded, shipping barely moved.
body: According to X's news summary, an NBER study of more than 500,000 GitHub developers found AI agents drove 240% more commits, 80% more projects and seven times more lines of code. Releases rose only 30%, and repo abandonment climbed from 60% to 69%. New apps in the major stores have doubled since early 2025 while total user engagement held flat.

Developer Andre Barbera's summary went viral: "25x more code, 30% more launches, same number of users." The debate splits between people who see agents as a prototyping superpower and people warning that maintenance and shipping still need human judgment.

stories.headline: OpenRouter off-boards three inference providers after data-policy violations surface
stories.why_read: If you route traffic through OpenRouter (you track its leaderboard every Monday), this is the operational fine print.
body: OpenRouter says security researchers found that certain inference providers had data compromised or were not upholding their stated data policies. OpenRouter itself was not breached. In response it off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, including some taken out as a precaution, and notified potentially affected customers.

It is now adapting the researchers' tests to run continuously, verifying network paths to catch requests and responses being forwarded to third parties, and requiring assurances before any endpoint gets ZDR status back. The lesson for anyone building on hosted models: a provider's data policy is only as good as someone's ability to test it.

stories.headline: Sunny Madra: FSD swerved out of a crash this week; the car took damage but avoided worse
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: a real-world save, posted with video, the same week v15 claims 25x better safety handling.
body: Sunny Madra posted two clips of what he called a crazy accident early this week, in which FSD swerved out of the way. His car took some damage, he says, but avoided something much more serious.
It is one anecdote, not a statistic, but it is the kind of footage that shapes how people feel about letting the car drive.

stories.headline: "FSD is GTA irl": the first v15 owner clips, from garages to a Costco lot
stories.why_read: You retweeted almost a dozen of these last night: the fun side of the release.
body: Within hours of the rollout, owners were posting clips. Sawyer Merritt says v15 pulled straight into his garage for the first time ever, and that the bird's-eye view helps at a drive-through by showing the curb edge and even filled-in road cracks. TruthTom shows it steering around a huge branch in the road and pulling to the right of a car in his driveway. BLKMDL3 says it let him choose which Costco lot to park in.
Elon Musk's caption on the branch clip summed up the mood: "FSD is GTA irl." X's news summary adds that car dealership insiders are quietly impressed, with some urging legacy brands to license it.

stories.headline: California is the "final boss" for robotaxi approval, and Tesla is already testing there
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the regulatory map for where Cybercab can go next.
body: James Cat argues the approval pathway for fully autonomous robotaxis in California is much more demanding than in Florida or Texas, making the state "basically the final boss in autonomy."
He notes Tesla is already testing there with a safety driver, and that Elon Musk says Tesla will have a California robotaxi next year.

stories.headline: Musk says Optimus goes to mines and refineries first, not your kitchen
stories.why_read: Where the humanoid economics actually work: round-the-clock heavy industry.
body: At the November 18 TomorrowX Summit, Elon Musk described deploying Optimus in mining and ore refining, where nonstop operation lets one robot rack up enormous productive hours, according to X's news summary. Early production is ramping at Fremont, with external deliveries eyed for late 2027.
Household chores such as washing, drying and putting away dishes come later; Musk puts those 12 to 18 months out, citing recent gains in hand dexterity.

stories.headline: HSBC doubles its Tesla target to $359 on SpaceX merger speculation
stories.why_read: A bank modeling what a SpaceX-Tesla combination would be worth, per share.
body: HSBC analyst Michael Tyndall upgraded Tesla to Hold and raised his price target from $157 to $359, X's news summary reports. His blended model values Tesla at $507 per share if SpaceX buys it at a 33% premium, or $212 standalone on vehicles, energy and autonomy.
Musk has noted the growing overlap in AI, robotics and chip design, while stressing high shareholder approval hurdles and that SpaceX doesn't need Tesla.

stories.headline: Report: 87% of Anthropic's power could come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
stories.why_read: Energy tech from your pinned post, meeting the AI buildout head-on.
body: The Better Data Center Project ran a case study of Anthropic's total power use and estimates the company could emit 32 million metric tons of CO2 in 2028. Its headline breakdown: 87% of that power from gas and 11% from coal.

The broader context from the same group: 177 GW of planned "bring your own power" gas capacity at data centers, with renewables under 20% of that generation through 2032, plus another 200 GW of new fossil plants being built on the grid, largely because of data centers.

stories.headline: LLMs can now read and write executables byte by byte from a hex dump
stories.why_read: For a systems person, this is a strange new capability: no disassembler, no compiler, just bytes.
body: George Xenos and Sotiris Giannopoulos gave GPT-6.1 Sol only hex dumps and no tools. It explained all five binaries, including a stripped open-source statistics tool where it found a real upstream bug, analyzed an unknown malware sample and extracted the correct indicators of compromise, added features to three binaries by editing their bytes, and wrote three programs from scratch.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reached the same conclusion about the malware, a hint that this is not limited to closed models. The authors float the idea that models may eventually write machine code directly instead of high-level languages.

stories.headline: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
stories.why_read: A great networking whodunit, the kind of debugging story you love.
body: Oscar Molnar has a 2.5 Gbps symmetrical line but saw only 600 Mbps down after moving his Ethernet adapter onto his Studio Display XDR for a one-cable setup. Pings during downloads failed 10% of the time with no dropped-frame errors logged by macOS, which told him the adapter was dropping frames before the Mac ever saw them. Plugged straight into the Mac, the same adapter hit 2.3 Gbps.

Realtek's own driver nearly doubled speed but still fell short. The fix was a newer adapter whose USB burst size is twice as large, so its buffer never fills behind the display's hub and no frames drop. The write-up walks through the flow-control math.

stories.headline: Upload2Shell: a Ghostscript font-loader bug escapes the -dSAFER sandbox
stories.why_read: Ghostscript hides under print, email, upload and preview pipelines, including ones that think they only handle images.
body: pwn.ai disclosed CVE-2026-125396, a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader that lets a crafted document cross the -dSAFER sandbox, alter native path controls and run attacker-chosen commands as the rendering process.

Their earlier ImageMagick work showed how files named .png or .jpg can still reach Ghostscript through image conversion, and the disclosure includes an index of confirmed affected application paths. Worth a check of any service that renders user uploads.

stories.headline: Raph Levien's advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
stories.why_read: A thoughtful systems essay, updated for a world where AI is fueling a rush of new toolkits.
body: Four and a half years after his advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, Raph Levien counts roughly 20 toolkits announced since, and a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI fueled by AI.

His case is that the motivation is stronger than ever: platform toolkits have stagnated, Electron keeps growing, and with RAM expensive and focus shifting to mobile, bloat has real consequences. Adoption has been slow so far, and the post is about what new toolkits should do differently.

stories.headline: gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go
stories.why_read: A neat tool for anyone who has wanted Postgres extensions without writing C.
body: gopgext uses TinyGo to compile PostgreSQL extensions from ordinary Go code. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function; the tool writes the C glue, the install script and the control file, and much of the standard library works.
The author is clear it is experimental: a bug in generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the database server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, so keep it away from production for now.

stories.headline: unkernel: a real Linux kernel compiled to WebAssembly that boots in under a second
stories.why_read: Linux itself, not an emulator, running in a browser tab.
body: unkernel is Linux 7.x built as a single WebAssembly module with a real MMU. The kernel, including syscalls, the scheduler, memory management, ext4 and TCP/IP, is compiled code rather than emulated, so programs get Linux's own behavior down to the edge cases.
Only user programs are emulated: unmodified arm64 Linux binaries, so Alpine and Debian packages run as they are. It boots to a shell in less than a second and ships a JavaScript SDK.

stories.headline: A chart puts Starship launch costs near $20 per kilogram by 2036, and Musk agrees
stories.why_read: The number that makes orbital data centers and factories plausible.
body: A widely shared chart traces Starship launch costs from over $1,000 per kilogram in 2026 to about $20 by 2036, on full reuse of both stages and higher flight rates, against Falcon 9's current near-$3,000 per kilogram, per X's news summary.
Elon Musk replied simply: "Yeah, mass to orbit will get ridiculously cheap." His stated goal for mature operations is under $100 per kilogram.

stories.headline: Musk pitches solar-powered "computronium" on the Moon, then Mercury
stories.why_read: Energy and compute physics at the most ambitious scale imaginable.
body: Responding to a discussion about powering AI, Elon Musk argued it is easier to generate solar energy and run advanced computing in space, and suggested converting parts of the Moon, then Mercury, into computronium built from silicon solar cells and aluminum radiators, per X's news summary.

Grok chimed in that Mercury gets six to nine times Earth's sunlight and has the raw materials, starting with lunar mass drivers. Replies mixed "It's always sunny in space" memes with real questions about heat rejection and debris.

stories.headline: Boom says it has made both a supersonic airplane and a supersonic engine
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a rare vertical-integration milestone in aviation.
body: Blake Scholl notes that extremely few companies have made both an engine and an airplane, and none had made a supersonic airplane and a supersonic engine "until today."
"Today a new engine company was born," he writes, sharing a launch video best watched with the volume up.

stories.headline: Toyota, Nissan and Honda will standardize parts to cut costs
stories.why_read: Rivals cooperating on the boring stuff, under pressure from cheaper competitors.
body: Japan's three biggest automakers will start standardizing some vehicle parts, Car and Driver reports, citing Automotive News. They begin with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.
The decision was announced by Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, also vice chairman of Toyota. Talks start with domestic suppliers, with international suppliers to follow.

stories.headline: Fix bad Wi-Fi in five minutes by asking your Bot, and next it calls your ISP
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it, and it is exactly how you use your own fleet of bots.
body: Matt Palmer shared a simple flow: tell your Bot "help me fix my wifi per this post," it optimizes the Wi-Fi right away, finds a separate network issue, and tells you to call your provider. "The next step is to have Bot call your ISP for you!"

X's news summary says early Grok Bot users are deploying it for email checks, market analysis, coding and Slack coordination, with one calling it underpriced compared to a small team, though some run into usage limits.

stories.headline: How to automate anything with an agent, in four steps
stories.why_read: You retweeted Ben Holmes on Poteto's essay and Greg Hickman on Notion's "A New Shape for Work": the playbook for your bot fleet.
body: Ben Holmes says Poteto's article puts automation in simple terms: state the goal; outline your process today, with as much context as possible; design the automation with access to your tools; and connect signals like customer feedback or time to PR so the agent can improve itself.

Greg Hickman makes a related case from Notion's "A New Shape for Work": put everything your team knows in one shared place so you and your AI stop starting from scratch, link clients, projects and meetings so any person or agent can find the full picture, and turn each repeatable deliverable into a "factory."

stories.headline: "The worst tech drawdown since 2003," while memory stays sold out through 2029
stories.why_read: Two charts you bookmarked and saw in your feed tell opposite stories about the same AI buildout.
body: ARK's Brett Winton posted a chart calling this the worst tech drawdown since 2003.

On the other side, François Chollet pointed to HBM and DRAM sold out through 2029, with compute demand doubling every five months and inference needs rising fast, per X's news summary. Whether this is the end of the run or a buying window is now the whole debate.

stories.headline: Five rules for parenting teenagers: drive them places and stay up late
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the love-and-kindness slot, from a dad who has raised a few.
body: Justin Hart's advice: drive them places, because they talk in the car. Stay up late, because the real stuff comes out after 10 pm. Feed their friends.
And the two that are hardest: say "I was wrong" out loud, because they'll copy it, and don't win every argument. Let them see you change your mind.

stories.headline: Before it was the James Bond theme, it was a song for an Indo-Trinidadian musical
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a delightful bit of music history with an Indian connection.
body: The Juggernaut tells the story: when Albert Broccoli asked Monty Norman to compose the 007 theme, Norman went back to a song with "traditional Indian instruments" he had written for A House for Mr. Biswas, an unstaged musical.
That melody went on to become one of the most recognizable themes in film.

stories.headline: Cold front Tuesday, but no snow in Austin
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: the local forecast for your week.
body: Meteorologist Tommy House says a cold front moves through Tuesday with limited moisture. Some computer models want wintry weather closer to the Hill Country, but it doesn't pass his eye test.
There could be some flakes in West Texas and the Panhandle; Central Texas gets all rain. His verdict: "NO snow in Austin!"
